objectives: I can explain the nature and need for abstraction: removing detail irrelevant to the problem
I can distinguish representational abstraction from generalisation, with a valid example of each
I can compare an abstraction with reality and justify which details are kept or discarded for a purpose
I can devise an abstract model for a given real-world scenario

retrieval.q: From 1.1.1: describe the first two steps of the fetch stage, naming the registers.
retrieval.a: The contents of the PC are copied into the MAR; the instruction is fetched from that address via the data bus into the MDR.

retrieval.q: From 1.1.1: state the key difference between Von Neumann and Harvard architecture.
retrieval.a: Von Neumann has one shared memory and bus for data and instructions; Harvard has separate memories and buses for each.

retrieval.q: From 1.1.1: a CPU has a 16-bit address bus. How many locations can it address?
From 1.1.2: which RISC feature makes pipelining easier, and why?
retrieval.a: Fixed-length, simple instructions taking one cycle each, so every pipeline stage takes a predictable, equal time.
Using a GPU for general-purpose, non-graphics computation such as machine learning or scientific simulation.

keywords.def: Removing or hiding detail irrelevant to the problem so only relevant information remains, giving a simpler model.
Simplifying one specific thing into a model of that problem, e.g. a road network as a graph.
Grouping many things by shared characteristics into one reusable model, e.g. one Account type for all accounts.
A simplified representation of a real-world thing or system, built for a purpose.
A model keeping only the data and behaviour needed to solve the stated problem.
A point in a graph abstraction, such as a junction, station or place.
A connection between nodes carrying a cost such as distance or time.
Breaking a problem into smaller sub-problems; a different skill from abstraction.

content.heading: What abstraction is
points: Abstraction removes or hides unnecessary detail so only information relevant to the problem remains
The result is a simpler model that is easier to understand, build and reason about
You met it constantly in 1.1: a register diagram ignores transistors; block diagrams hide wiring
The skill being examined: deciding WHAT to remove, and justifying why it is safe

content.heading: Why we need abstraction
points: Real systems have overwhelming detail; keeping all of it makes solutions impossibly complex
Removing irrelevant detail makes systems simpler, faster to build and easier to maintain
Programmers work at the right layer: a variable is an abstraction of a memory address
Users benefit too: an interface hides the implementation underneath

content.heading: Type 1: representational abstraction
points: Simplifies ONE specific thing into a model of that problem
Example: a road network becomes a graph of nodes (junctions) and weighted edges (distances or times)
Example: the London Underground map, a game minimap, a flight simulator's simplified physics
Test question: am I stripping detail from one particular thing?

content.heading: Type 2: generalisation (categorisation)
points: Groups MANY things by their shared characteristics into one reusable model
Example: savings and current accounts handled by one Account type
Example: a Vehicle record covering cars, vans and bikes in a rental system
Test question: am I finding what many things have in common?
content.note: Exams expect BOTH types distinguished, each with a valid example.

content.heading: Abstraction versus reality
points: An abstraction always contains less detail than the real thing it models
The Tube map discards true geography and scale but keeps lines, station order and interchanges
It is not wrong: it perfectly serves the purpose of planning which line to take
Two correct abstractions of the same thing can look completely different if their purposes differ

content.heading: Keep or discard? It depends on the purpose
points: There is no universal list of irrelevant detail; relevance is relative to the stated problem
For a journey planner, live bus GPS is irrelevant; for a where-is-my-bus app it is essential
A good answer names specific data to keep, specific detail to discard, and justifies each discard
Removing a NECESSARY detail breaks the model: a canteen map without the turnings fails its user
content.note: The justification of each discarded detail usually carries the mark, not the list itself.

content.heading: Devising an abstract model: a method
points: State the problem precisely: what questions must the model answer?
List candidate details of the real thing, then sort into keep and discard against that problem
Choose a representation for what is kept: variables, records, a graph of nodes and edges
Check: can the model still answer every question the problem asks? If yes, stop adding detail

content.heading: Worked pattern: real world to graph
points: Many problems reduce to places and connections: roads, flight routes, social networks, network cables
Keep: the points (nodes) and which pairs connect (edges) with a cost (weights)
Discard: scenery, road names, curve shapes — none change the shortest route
This one abstraction lets one algorithm (shortest path) solve every such problem

content.heading: Abstraction is NOT decomposition
points: Abstraction removes or hides detail to simplify a model
Decomposition breaks a problem into smaller sub-problems
They are different skills, examined separately, and often confused
One sentence check: removing detail = abstraction; splitting into parts = decomposition

content.heading: The payoff: benefits to name in answers
points: Simpler model: quicker to design, build and test
Easier to maintain: less code and fewer places for bugs to hide
Generalised models are easy to extend: new cases reuse the existing model instead of new code
Always tie an abstraction answer back to one of these benefits

worked_examples.title: Abstracting a patient for a hospital appointments system
steps: Problem: schedule appointments and contact patients about them
Keep: patient ID and name, date of birth, contact number, GP or clinic, appointment type and duration — each is needed to schedule or to contact the patient
Discard: eye colour, favourite food, home decor
Justify each discard: none of these affect scheduling or contacting the patient, so including them adds complexity without value
Conclusion: keeping only relevant detail makes the system simpler, quicker to build and easier to maintain while still solving the appointments problem

worked_examples.title: Devising a model: sat-nav road network as a weighted graph
steps: Problem: find the fastest route between two locations
Keep: junctions and places as nodes; roads between them as edges; average travel time on each road as the edge weight
Discard: road surface colour, buildings, scenery, the exact curve of each road — they do not change which route is fastest
Represent: a graph where the fastest route is the path with the lowest total weight
Check the purpose: to show turn-by-turn directions we must also keep junction names — necessary detail depends on the exact problem
Classify: this is representational abstraction (one specific network simplified), though the graph idea itself generalises to any network

worked_examples.title: Classifying examples: representational or generalisation?
steps: Apply the test question: one thing simplified, or many things grouped by shared features?
The Tube map: one specific network with detail stripped — representational
An Animal superclass for Dog, Cat and Horse: many things grouped by shared characteristics — generalisation
A weather model ignoring individual raindrops: one system simplified — representational
Treating all customers as name, ID and balance: many people reduced to shared fields — generalisation
Takeaway: write the test question in your answer; it shows the examiner your reasoning

activities.title: Map to the Canteen
instructions: Without discussion, each student draws directions from this classroom to the canteen for a brand-new Year 7; five minutes, no style rules given
Pairs swap and mentally walk the route, listing what details are on the map and what real-world details were left out (wall colours, door widths, exact distances, rooms passed)
Class harvest in two columns, kept versus discarded, then the key question: why was each discarded detail safe to remove? Because it does not change whether the Year 7 arrives

Introduce the definition only after the experience: abstraction = removing or hiding unnecessary detail so only relevant information remains; show a floor plan or satellite photo — the map is not wrong, it serves a different purpose
Twist round: redraw for a different purpose, a wheelchair user or a fire-evacuation plan; what must be added back (lifts, ramps, all exits) and what can now go?
activities.stretch: Name the map's interface (the instructions followed) versus its hidden implementation (the actual building), and connect this to a variable being an abstraction of a memory address.

activities.title: Representational or Generalisation? Card Sort
instructions: Pairs sort ten example cards under two headers: representational abstraction (remove detail from one specific thing) and generalisation (group many things by shared characteristics)

Cards: the Tube map; an Animal superclass for Dog, Cat, Horse; a road network as a graph of nodes and weighted edges; a Vehicle record for cars, vans and bikes; a weather model ignoring raindrops; savings and current accounts under one Account type; a game minimap; a Shape class with area() overridden by Circle and Square; a flight simulator's simplified physics; all customers as name, ID, balance
Pairs must write the test question they used to decide (one thing simplified, or many things grouped?)
Class check: representational = Tube map, road graph, weather model, minimap, simulator; generalisation = Animal, Vehicle, Account, Shape, customers
Pairs generate one new example of each type from a video game they know
activities.stretch: Identify a card that is arguably both (the road-network graph simplifies one map AND generalises places-plus-connections to any network) and defend the dual reading.

activities.title: Always, Sometimes, Never: Abstraction Claims
instructions: Give pairs seven statement slips: (a) an abstraction contains less detail than the real thing; (b) removing more detail makes an abstraction better; (c) abstraction and decomposition are the same skill; (d) two correct abstractions of the same thing can look completely different; (e) a model that leaves out relevant detail is a poor abstraction for that problem; (f) abstraction is only used in programming; (g) the Tube map is wrong because distances are not to scale
Pairs classify each as Always, Sometimes or Never with a one-line justification and an example
Pairs merge into fours; disagreements must be settled by constructing a counter-example
Debrief targeting (b) and (c), the two most commonly botched in exams

Answers: (a) Always; (b) Sometimes — remove a necessary detail and the model stops working; (c) Never — abstraction removes detail, decomposition splits into sub-problems; (d) Always possible — different purposes; (e) Always; (f) Never — maps, timetables, models everywhere; (g) Never — it is fit for its purpose, scale is the discarded detail
activities.stretch: Fours draft one new Sometimes statement whose truth hinges on the problem's purpose, and challenge another four.

practice.a: Removing or hiding unnecessary detail (1) so that only information relevant to the problem remains, giving a simpler model (1).

practice.q: Explain one reason why abstraction is needed when developing software. [2]
practice.a: Real-world systems contain overwhelming amounts of detail (1); removing what is irrelevant makes the program simpler, faster to develop and easier to test and maintain (1).

practice.q: Describe the difference between representational abstraction and generalisation, giving an example of each. [4]
practice.a: Representational abstraction simplifies one specific thing into a model of that problem (1), e.g. a road network stored as a graph of nodes and weighted edges, or the Tube map (1); generalisation groups many things by shared characteristics into one reusable model (1), e.g. savings and current accounts treated as a single Account type (1).

practice.q: A developer is creating a route-finding app. Describe how the real road network could be represented as an abstract model. [3]
practice.a: Junctions and places become nodes (1); roads between them become edges weighted with distance or travel time (1); irrelevant detail such as scenery, buildings and the exact shapes of roads is discarded because it does not affect the choice of route (1).

practice.q: A program models a library member for a book-loans system. State two pieces of data the model should keep and two details of the real person it should discard, justifying the discards. [4]
practice.a: Keep: member ID/name and contact details, plus current loans/due dates (1 for two sensible items); these are needed to record and chase loans (1). Discard: e.g. hair colour and favourite author (1); neither affects recording or returning loans, so they add complexity without value (1).

practice.q: The London Underground map does not show true distances or geography. Explain why it is still a good abstraction. [3]
practice.a: Its purpose is to help passengers plan which lines to take and where to change (1); it keeps the relevant detail — lines, station order and interchanges (1) — and discards geography and scale, which do not affect that decision, making it clearer to use (1).

practice.q: A student says that abstraction means breaking a problem down into smaller sub-problems. Explain why the student is wrong. [2]
practice.a: Breaking a problem into sub-problems is decomposition, a different computational thinking skill (1); abstraction is removing or hiding detail irrelevant to the problem to produce a simpler model (1).

practice.q: A bank replaces separate savings-account and current-account code with a single generalised Account model. Explain two benefits of this generalisation. [4]
practice.a: Shared behaviour (deposit, withdraw, check balance) is written once instead of twice, reducing code size and the chance of inconsistent bugs (1) and making maintenance easier since fixes apply everywhere (1); the system is easier to extend, because a new account type can reuse the existing model rather than needing new code from scratch (1), cutting development time and testing effort (1).

misconceptions: Students often think abstraction and decomposition are the same, but abstraction removes detail while decomposition splits a problem into sub-problems.
Students often think removing more detail always improves a model, but removing a necessary detail stops the model solving its problem.
Students often think the Tube map is a wrong or bad map, but a model is judged against its purpose, and scale is the deliberately discarded detail.
Students often define abstraction instead of applying it; exam marks come from naming scenario-specific details kept and discarded, with justification.
Students often think abstraction only happens in code, but maps, timetables and physics models are everyday abstractions.
exam_link: Command words: Define/State (2 marks), Describe (a model for a scenario, 3-4 marks), Explain (why abstraction helps here, 2-4 marks), Discuss (use of abstraction across a whole system, up to 9-mark levels of response).
Application beats recitation: examiners give scenario marks for named details kept and discarded WITH justification, not for a memorised definition alone.
Example stem: 'A developer is writing a fitness-tracking app. Describe how abstraction will have been used in the design of the app.' — answer with specific kept/discarded data.
The abstraction/decomposition mix-up is an established trap; one sentence distinguishing them can secure a mark.
task: Devise an abstract model for a school parents-evening booking system. List at least four pieces of data to keep and four real-world details to discard, justify every discard against the booking problem, and state whether your teacher and parent records are representational abstraction or generalisation, and why.
challenge: Take your parents-evening model and change the problem to fire-safety roll call during an evacuation of the event. Write down which discarded details must now return, which kept details become irrelevant, and one sentence explaining what this shows about abstraction being relative to purpose.

exit_ticket.q: In one sentence, what is abstraction?
exit_ticket.a: Removing or hiding detail irrelevant to the problem so only relevant information remains, giving a simpler model.

exit_ticket.q: Give the test question that separates representational abstraction from generalisation.
exit_ticket.a: Am I stripping detail from one specific thing (representational) or grouping many things by shared characteristics (generalisation)?

exit_ticket.q: How is abstraction different from decomposition?
exit_ticket.a: Abstraction removes or hides detail; decomposition breaks a problem into smaller sub-problems.
